title: Tenancy routing spectrum — operator notes and checklist
content:
Purpose:
This is an operator-facing note that maps the tenancy/routing spectrum for Redwood deployments (hosted / dedicated / private), calls out practical isolation boundaries, and provides an onboarding + ops checklist. The goal: reduce ambiguity in who enforces what (control plane vs dataplane), and give runbooks for common failure modes when routing / capacity / region decisions diverge.

Quick overview / TL;DR:
- Hosted: control plane owns global routing decisions; strong multitenant dataplane isolation but flexible routing policies (global spill, cheap fallbacks).
- Dedicated: tenant-pinned capacity; control plane delegates routing to per-tenant schedulers; stricter capacity isolation, limited global failover.
- Private (VPC / on-prem): customer control plane or hybrid; routing is customer-managed or policy-led; we provide routing primitives and best-effort recommendations.

Definitions / axes to think about:
- Control plane authority: who can change routing decisions (Redwood control plane, tenant control plane, customer-managed).
- Data-plane isolation: shared GPUs vs tenant-reserved nodes; network egress separation; KV cache tenancy.
- Failover semantics: automatic region fallback, cross-tenant spill, or reject-on-limit.
- Trust envelope: which party has access to telemetry, tracing, prompts, full logs.

Routing pattern catalog (short):
1) Global-proxy routing (Hosted default): front-end edge decides region+model variant, routes to multi-tenant pools. Pros: latency/cost optimization, transparent fallbacks. Cons: requires strong SLOs, careful tenant isolation.
2) Tenant-affinity pinning (Dedicated): tokens map to tenant cluster; control plane TTL for pins; ideal for predictable throughput.
3) Customer-controlled routing (Private): customer config (BGP/VPC endpoint + routing table); Redwood agent enforces model compatibility and rollout policies.
4) Hybrid threshold-spill: tenant pinned to dedicated pool until CPU/GPU saturated, then optionally spill to hosted pool under strict data governance constraints.

Isolation boundaries — practical checklist:
- Authentication/Identity: edge token -> tenant id. Control plane must validate token scoping before any routing decision.
- Metadata propagation: 'tenant_id', 'data_class' (sensitive/non-sensitive), 'route_policy' must be attached and immutable after edge.
- KV / prefix cache: per-tenant namespaces; never allowed to be shared across tenant nodes. (Enforce via FS mounts / process isolation.)
- Network egress: Dedicated and Private require tenant-specific NAT or egress proxies. Hosted uses shared egress but must support allowlists and per-tenant egress tagging.
- Telemetry scrub: hosted control plane aggregates traces; for Private we only receive anonymized SLO pings unless customer opts-in.

Operator scenarios and recommended actions:
A) Latency spike for tenant on Hosted despite healthy global capacity:
  - Check edge routing hot-spotting (requests pinned to single AZ).
  - Validate prefix cache hit ratio; a low KV cache hit leads to longer cold KV loads.
  - If autoscaler is slow, temporarily enable short-term burst to Dedicated-like nodes.
B) Tenant exceeds committed throughput on Dedicated and is throttled:
  - Verify spill policy: if "spill_enabled" and data_class != sensitive then allow temporary spill to hosted pool; otherwise notify tenant and enforce limit.
  - Trigger capacity-ordering SLA path: create capacity ticket (JIRA PLT-xxxxx) and pre-warm nodes.
C) Private deployment cross-region failover test failing:
  - Confirm routing entries propagated (BGP / route-reflector) and health-check endpoints allowed across VPC peering.
  - Verify agent versions between control planes; mismatched pruning logic can drop stateful KV caches.

Operational checks before onboarding new tenant (short checklist):
- Has tenant signed data policy (sensitive vs standard)? (yes/no)
- Required SLAs: latency P99, throughput QPS (numbers)
- Routing mode preference: hosted / dedicated / private / hybrid
- Spill policy: allowed? yes/no; constraints (regions, model variants)
- Egress requirements: allowlist / dedicated NAT / HSM requirements
- Monitoring hooks: trace keys, log retention, alert contacts
- Test plan: synthetic traffic, cold-start trace capture, KV-keyspace sanity checks

Design trade-offs and guidance notes:
- Strong isolation (Dedicated) increases unit-cost but reduces blast radius and simplifies compliance. Operationally, Dedicated reduces routing complexity at the edge (token -> cluster).
- Hosted routing is where our cost and latency advantages live, but needs extremely clear metadata/capability contracts to avoid cross-tenant leaks.
- Hybrid spill is valuable commercially (sell overage flexibility) but operationally risky: define narrow, auditable paths and automatic retraction when capacity normalizes.

Instrumentation / metrics to watch (suggested):
- Per-tenant routing latency histogram (edge → model endpoint).
- Prefix cache hit ratio over time per tenant.
- Spill count and spill latency (how often do requests leave the pinned pool).
- Token-to-cluster mapping churn (how often pins change).
- Control plane route decision latency (ms): time from token validation to route push.

Outstanding TODOs / questions:
- Do we want tenant-level SLA annotations on the global routing engine (so operators can filter decisions by SLA class)?
- How granular should spill policies be (model-version, data-class, region)?
- For private installs where we have an agent, what minimum telemetry must it return to keep routing safety checks working without violating customer privacy?

Appendix — quick sample policies (pseudo):
- policy: "no-spill-sensitive" => if data_class == sensitive then always reject cross-tenant spill routes.
- policy: "spill-with-ack" => on spill, log request id and require downstream ACK within 2s or revert.

Notes to self / rough action items:
- Draft a consolidated Confluence doc mapping 'policy->metric->alert' for oncall. (assigned: Daniel P.)
- Add a checkbox in the onboarding flow to sign 'spill agreement' document. (Maya R.)
- Create unit tests for token->tenant pin-churn to make sure we don't overrotate pins under load (JIRA PLT-3072).

References:
- Confluence design: CONFLUENCE-PLATFORM-4821 (routing policy primer)
- GitHub PR: routing-policy-proto/pull/88 (policy schema v2)
